chapter_title: Unit Testing and Test-Driven Development (TDD) in C++

screens.title: Unit Testing & TDD in C++
screens.subtitle: Practical unit tests with Google Test and the Red-Green-Refactor workflow

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why unit testing matters for C++ projects and how Test-Driven Development shapes better code. Unit tests check individual functions, methods, or classes in isolation so bugs surface early. We’ll use Google Test because it gives expressive assertions, test fixtures, and a familiar workflow for C++ developers. You’ll see how to write tests for simple functions, use fixtures to manage setup and teardown, and follow the TDD cycle of Red, Green, Refactor when building a Stack data structure. Along the way we’ll highlight common anti-patterns like testing implementation details or over-mocking, and show strategies to keep tests independent and maintainable. By the end, you should be able to write focused tests that document behavior, run them via CMake, and use tests as a safety net when refactoring. Think of tests as living documentation: they describe how code must behave and let you change internals without fear. Are you ready to build reliable C++ code one test at a time?

First, you will understand the principles and benefits of unit testing in C++: how tests find regressions early, support refactoring, and serve as living documentation. Second, you will learn to write effective unit tests using Google Test, including common assertions and how to structure test suites so each test verifies a single behavior. Third, you will implement and use test fixtures to manage setup and teardown, ensuring each test runs in a clean environment and avoids hidden dependencies. Finally, you will practice Test-Driven Development: write a failing test first, implement the minimal code to pass it, and then refactor. Each objective includes a concrete example or mnemonic to make the skill actionable. These competencies help you design safer APIs, write clearer tests, and move faster with confidence when changing code.

screens.title: What is Unit Testing?
screens.subtitle: Definition, scope, and practical benefits for C++ projects

narration.text: Unit testing means testing the smallest testable pieces of code—functions, methods, or classes—in isolation. In C++ that usually translates to compiling small test suites that exercise a function or class, verifying outputs and side effects under controlled inputs. The practical benefits are straightforward: tests catch regressions early, let you refactor internals confidently, and serve as executable documentation of expected behavior. For example, a small add function tested across positive, negative, and zero inputs documents the intended arithmetic behavior and guards against future changes that break it. A common misconception is that unit testing duplicates integration testing; instead, unit tests focus on one unit’s contract, while integration tests verify interactions between components. Another pitfall is writing tests that assert implementation details rather than observable behavior; such tests become brittle when you refactor. To avoid that, assert on returned values, public side effects, or thrown exceptions. In short, unit tests are compact, fast, and meant to provide immediate feedback during development. If you keep tests small and behavior-focused, they will speed development rather than slow it. What is Unit Testing? means test individual units in isolation to document behavior and detect regressions early.. In practical terms, definition, scope, and practical benefits for c++ projects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Unit Testing Defined
keyIdea.text: Test individual units in isolation to document behavior and detect regressions early.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › What is Unit Testing?
Definition & Scope

Unit testing verifies the smallest testable units of code in isolation. Tests are fast, focused, and designed to run frequently during development.

Benefits
  • Early bug detection and regression prevention
  • Easier refactoring with safety nets
  • Executable documentation of behavior
Common misconception
Unit tests are not integration tests. They should not verify inter-module wiring; that belongs in higher-level tests.
Example: add(int a, int b)
// calculator.h
#pragma once
int add(int a, int b);

// calculator.cpp
#include "calculator.h"
int add(int a, int b) {
  return a + b;
}

// calculator_test.cpp
#include "gtest/gtest.h"
#include "calculator.h"

TEST(CalculatorFunctions, HandlesPositiveNumbers) {
  EXPECT_EQ(5, add(2, 3));
  EXPECT_EQ(10, add(5, 5));
}
Key Takeaway

Keep tests behavior-focused, fast, and independent so they provide quick feedback during development.

screens.title: Google Test Basics
screens.subtitle: TEST, TEST_F, and the assertion family

narration.text: Google Test provides a lightweight way to express expectations about behavior in C++. At the simplest level you use TEST to declare a standalone test case and give it a descriptive name. When multiple tests share common setup and cleanup code, you use TEST_F with a fixture class that inherits from ::testing::Test. Fixtures allow you to implement SetUp and TearDown to prepare the same environment for each test. Assertions are the language of verification: EXPECT_* records a failure and continues executing the test, while ASSERT_* aborts the current test early if the condition is critical for subsequent checks. Use EXPECT when you can meaningfully continue checking other aspects of behavior, and ASSERT when a failed check would make later assertions meaningless or unsafe. The test example for add demonstrates EXPECT_EQ to compare values. For exceptional cases, use ASSERT_THROW or EXPECT_THROW to verify that code signals errors correctly. The right assertion choice keeps test reports clear and helps you diagnose failures quickly. Google Test Basics means use test for simple checks, test_f with fixtures for shared setup, and choose expect vs assert depending on dependency between checks.. In practical terms, test, test_f, and the assertion family. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GTest essentials
keyIdea.text: Use TEST for simple checks, TEST_F with fixtures for shared setup, and choose EXPECT vs ASSERT depending on dependency between checks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Google Test Basics
TEST vs TEST_F

TEST declares a simple test. TEST_F uses a fixture class that can centralize SetUp and TearDown. Fixtures make many tests repeatable and independent.

Assertion types
  • EXPECT_EQ, EXPECT_TRUE — record failures and continue
  • ASSERT_EQ, ASSERT_TRUE — stop the current test immediately
  • EXPECT_THROW / ASSERT_THROW — verify exceptions
Best practice
Prefer EXPECT_* unless later assertions would be invalidated; keep each test focused on a single behavior.
Example: Fixture and assertions
#include "gtest/gtest.h"

class CalculatorTest : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
  void SetUp() override { /* prepare common objects */ }
  void TearDown() override { /* clean up */ }
};

TEST_F(CalculatorTest, CanAddTwoNumbers) {
  EXPECT_EQ(5, 2 + 3);
}

TEST(CalculatorFunctions, ThrowsOnBadInput) {
  ASSERT_THROW( /* call that should throw */, std::invalid_argument);
}
Key Takeaway

Match your assertion style to test flow: ASSERT when you must stop, EXPECT when you can continue checking other behavior.

screens.title: A Simple add() Test Suite
screens.subtitle: Readable tests that document expected behavior

narration.text: Let’s walk through the add example to see how tests document behavior. The header declares the function contract; the implementation returns a + b. The test file includes the Google Test header and the function's header, then defines several tests that exercise positive numbers, negatives, and zeros. Each TEST checks a single behavioral expectation using EXPECT_EQ. This structure shows three important ideas: tests express behavior through examples, they run quickly, and they provide immediate feedback when a change alters results. A helpful habit is to name tests descriptively, for example HandlesPositiveNumbers, HandlesNegativeNumbers, and HandlesZero. That naming makes the test report readable when a case fails. Also, expect multiple assertions per test only when they verify closely related aspects of a single behavior; otherwise split into separate tests. This example demonstrates fast, focused tests that will catch many simple mistakes and serve as documentation for how add should behave across input classes. A Simple add() Test Suite means use tests as examples: descriptive names and focused assertions make intent clear and failures actionable.. In practical terms, readable tests that document expected behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Express behavior
keyIdea.text: Use tests as examples: descriptive names and focused assertions make intent clear and failures actionable.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › A Simple add() Test Suite
Test file: calculator_test.cpp
#include "gtest/gtest.h"
#include "calculator.h" // Include the header for the function we want to test

TEST(CalculatorFunctions, HandlesPositiveNumbers) {
    EXPECT_EQ(5, add(2, 3));
    EXPECT_EQ(10, add(5, 5));
}

TEST(CalculatorFunctions, HandlesNegativeNumbers) {
    EXPECT_EQ(-5, add(-2, -3));
    EXPECT_EQ(0, add(-5, 5));
}

TEST(CalculatorFunctions, HandlesZero) {
    EXPECT_EQ(3, add(3, 0));
    EXPECT_EQ(-7, add(0, -7));
}
This set of tests verifies discrete input classes. The tests run quickly and form a compact specification for add().
Checklist
  • Name tests for clarity
  • Keep a test focused on one behavior
  • Use EXPECT for non-blocking checks
Key Takeaway

Tests should show expected behavior across representative inputs and clearly communicate intent when they fail.

screens.title: Test Fixtures: SetUp and TearDown
screens.subtitle: Creating a clean environment for multiple tests

narration.text: When multiple tests require the same objects or resources, test fixtures keep code DRY and tests independent. In Google Test you create a fixture by inheriting from ::testing::Test and defining SetUp() and TearDown() methods. SetUp runs before each test to create a fresh environment, and TearDown runs after each test to release resources. That means tests do not share mutable state and order dependency is removed. For example, when testing a Calculator or a database-backed component, the fixture can instantiate the object and reset any internal state so each test starts clean. Use TEST_F to attach tests to the fixture. A frequent misconception is to initialize a shared object once for all tests; this often causes hidden cross-test dependencies. Prefer per-test setup even if it repeats small allocations — test isolation is worth the cost. Fixtures also make it obvious where common test helpers live and simplify cleanup logic like closing connections or removing temporary files. Test Fixtures: SetUp and TearDown means setup and teardown guarantee a fresh environment for each test, preventing order-dependent failures.. In practical terms, creating a clean environment for multiple tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fixtures ensure isolation
keyIdea.text: SetUp and TearDown guarantee a fresh environment for each test, preventing order-dependent failures.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Test Fixtures
Fixture Example
#include "gtest/gtest.h"
#include "calculator.h"

class CalculatorTest : public ::testing::Test {
protected:
  Calculator calc; // used by every test
  void SetUp() override {
    // optional initialization
  }
  void TearDown() override {
    // optional cleanup
  }
};

TEST_F(CalculatorTest, CanAddTwoNumbers) {
  EXPECT_EQ(5, calc.add(2, 3));
}
This fixture gives each test a fresh Calculator instance. SetUp and TearDown make preparation and cleanup explicit and repeatable.
Why fixtures?
  • Avoid test interdependence
  • Centralize reusable setup code
  • Make cleanup deterministic
Common mistake
Sharing mutable state across tests because setup ran once leads to flaky suites. Prefer per-test initialization via SetUp.
Key Takeaway

Fixtures improve readability, reduce duplication, and ensure each test starts from a known state.

screens.title: TDD: Red → Green → Refactor
screens.subtitle: A disciplined cycle for designing testable code

narration.text: Test-Driven Development is a small-step process: Red, Green, Refactor. First, write a failing test that specifies the behavior you want — that’s Red. The failing test confirms that new behavior is missing. Second, make the test pass with the simplest, most direct implementation — that’s Green. Focus only on satisfying the test, not on perfect design. Third, refactor the code: remove duplication, improve names, and restructure internals while keeping tests passing. Refactoring is crucial because the Green step often introduces quick fixes or duplication that would otherwise accumulate into technical debt. A common pitfall is skipping refactor; without it code quality degrades. Another mistake is writing overly broad tests that assert multiple behaviors at once; instead, prefer small tests that guide incremental implementation. The TDD cycle drives A P I design from the outside in: tests define the contract first, which helps produce modular, testable components. Use the cycle iteratively to build up features with confidence. TDD: Red → Green → Refactor means write a failing test first, implement minimal code to pass it, then refactor safely with tests as a safety net.. In practical terms, a disciplined cycle for designing testable code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Red-Green-Refactor
keyIdea.text: Write a failing test first, implement minimal code to pass it, then refactor safely with tests as a safety net.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › TDD: Red → Green → Refactor
The TDD Cycle
Red
Write a failing test that specifies the next piece of behavior. The failure proves the test is meaningful.
Green
Implement the simplest code to make the test pass. Avoid overengineering.
Refactor
Improve design and remove duplication, keeping tests passing as a safety net.
TDD helps you design APIs from the outside in. A common error is writing large, complex tests that cover many behaviors; prefer incremental tests that lead to small, verifiable changes.
Tip

Keep red-green-refactor cycles short. Frequent, small cycles keep feedback immediate and design flexible.

screens.title: TDD Step 1: Red — IsEmptyInitially (Stack)
screens.subtitle: Write a failing test to drive the Stack API

narration.text: We begin the Stack TDD exercise by writing the first failing test: IsEmptyInitially. The test file includes Google Test and the stack header, which does not exist yet or is intentionally minimal. The test constructs a Stack and asserts that isEmpty() returns true. Attempting to compile should fail at first, verifying the test is meaningful. This Red step forces you to define the A P I contract: what methods exist and how they behave. Naming the test StackTest. IsEmptyInitially communicates intent. In practice, you add this test to test/test_stack. cpp and run your build; seeing the compile or test failure confirms you are driving design with tests. A common mistake here is to write too many assertions in the first test. Keep the test focused on a single behavior so that Green can implement the minimal change needed to satisfy it. TDD Step 1: Red — IsEmptyInitially (Stack) means a failing test confirms missing behavior and defines the api you will implement next.. In practical terms, write a failing test to drive the stack api. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Red: write the failing test
keyIdea.text: A failing test confirms missing behavior and defines the API you will implement next.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › TDD Step 1: Red — IsEmptyInitially
Initial failing test
// test/test_stack.cpp
#include "gtest/gtest.h"
#include "stack.h" // This will fail to compile initially

TEST(StackTest, IsEmptyInitially) {
    Stack s;
    EXPECT_TRUE(s.isEmpty());
}
Try compiling now. The missing or incomplete Stack API produces a failure, confirming the test is valuable and drives design.
Red Checklist
  • Keep the test minimal and focused
  • Name the test to reveal intent
  • Confirm the test fails before implementing
Avoid
Don't write large feature tests first. Small failing tests guide incremental design.

screens.title: TDD Step 2: Green — Implement isEmpty
screens.subtitle: Write the minimum code to satisfy the test

narration.text: After a failing test, implement the smallest amount of code that makes it pass. For the Stack example we add a Stack class with a constructor and an isEmpty method backed by std::vector. Keep the implementation minimal — no extra features yet. The goal of Green is correctness for the new test only. When you compile and run tests, IsEmptyInitially should pass. Resist the urge to generalize too early; generalization belongs in Refactor. Making this minimal change validates the A P I contract and gives you a working baseline to add further tests. This step underlines a TDD discipline: change just enough to pass tests, keep code readable, and let subsequent tests drive additional behavior. Running tests frequently keeps feedback immediate and helps isolate the effect of each change. TDD Step 2: Green — Implement isEmpty means implement only what the failing test requires so feedback stays focused and change is incremental.. In practical terms, write the minimum code to satisfy the test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Green: minimal implementation
keyIdea.text: Implement only what the failing test requires so feedback stays focused and change is incremental.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › TDD Step 2: Green — Implement isEmpty
Minimal Stack implementation
// src/stack.h
#pragma once
#include <vector>

class Stack {
public:
  Stack();
  bool isEmpty() const;
private:
  std::vector<int> data;
};

// src/stack.cpp
#include "stack.h"

Stack::Stack() {}

bool Stack::isEmpty() const { return data.empty(); }
Compile and run tests. The IsEmptyInitially test should now pass, giving a green signal for this behavior.
Green Checklist
  • Implement the minimal API to pass the test
  • Run the test suite often
  • Avoid premature generalization
Key Takeaway

Green proves the API and gives a safe starting point for adding the next test in the TDD cycle.

screens.title: TDD: Add push() and size() (Red → Green)
screens.subtitle: Grow the API through small failing tests and minimal fixes

narration.text: Once the initial isEmpty test passes, add the next behavior with a failing test: pushing an element should make the stack non-empty and increase size. Write a test that constructs a Stack, calls push(10), then expects isEmpty() to be false and size() to equal one. This Red test reveals the new A P I requirements: push and size methods. Implement these methods minimally by forwarding to the internal vector: push appends, size returns data. size. Run tests again; the new test should pass. The cycle continues: write a failing test for pop and peek next, and implement minimal functionality until those tests are green. This incremental approach surfaces A P I needs incrementally and prevents speculative design. Remember to assert a single behavior per test when possible. Each small test both documents and verifies one contract, making debugging simple when failures occur. TDD: Add push() and size() (Red → Green) means add one behavior at a time: write a failing test, implement minimal code, and repeat until the feature set is complete.. In practical terms, grow the api through small failing tests and minimal fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Grow by tests
keyIdea.text: Add one behavior at a time: write a failing test, implement minimal code, and repeat until the feature set is complete.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › TDD: push() and size()
Test: PushMakesStackNonEmptyAndIncreasesSize
TEST(StackTest, PushMakesStackNonEmptyAndIncreasesSize) {
    Stack s;
    s.push(10); // This method doesn't exist yet
    EXPECT_FALSE(s.isEmpty());
    EXPECT_EQ(1, s.size());
}
Minimal implementation: add push and size that use std::vector internally so the test becomes green.
// src/stack.h additions
void push(int value);
size_t size() const;

// src/stack.cpp additions
void Stack::push(int value) { data.push_back(value); }
size_t Stack::size() const { return data.size(); }
Testing tip
Run tests after each Green change. If a test fails, the failure is recent and easier to diagnose.
Key Takeaway

Incremental tests shape the API and reduce guesswork. Add one method at a time and prove it with tests.

screens.title: TDD: pop(), peek(), and exceptions
screens.subtitle: Handling edge cases and throwing on empty stack

narration.text: As you expand behavior, add tests for pop and peek and for error conditions. Write tests that push two elements, pop returns the last value and reduces size, and peek returns the top without removing it. Also write tests that expect std::out_of_range when popping or peeking on an empty stack. Implement pop and peek with checks and throw std::out_of_range when the stack is empty. These tests force you to handle edge cases explicitly instead of leaving undefined behavior. A common anti-pattern is to ignore edge cases during development; tests for boundary conditions prevent later surprises. After green, refactor: consider making Stack a template, improve exception messages, or centralize bounds checks into a helper. Refactor only once tests cover the behavior you want to keep. Tests for exceptions also act as documentation that certain misuse leads to well-defined errors. TDD: pop(), peek(), and exceptions means write tests for normal behavior and edge conditions; implement explicit exceptions to make failures predictable and documented.. In practical terms, handling edge cases and throwing on empty stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Edge cases matter
keyIdea.text: Write tests for normal behavior and edge conditions; implement explicit exceptions to make failures predictable and documented.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › TDD: pop(), peek(), and exceptions
Tests for pop and peek
TEST(StackTest, PopRemovesElementAndDecreasesSize) {
    Stack s;
    s.push(10);
    s.push(20);
    EXPECT_EQ(20, s.pop());
    EXPECT_EQ(1, s.size());
    EXPECT_EQ(10, s.pop());
    EXPECT_TRUE(s.isEmpty());
}

TEST(StackTest, PeekReturnsTopElementWithoutRemoving) {
    Stack s;
    s.push(10);
    s.push(20);
    EXPECT_EQ(20, s.peek());
    EXPECT_EQ(2, s.size());
}

TEST(StackTest, PopFromEmptyStackThrowsException) {
    Stack s;
    EXPECT_THROW(s.pop(), std::out_of_range);
}
Implement pop and peek to throw std::out_of_range when the stack is empty, and update tests until green.
Implementation snippet
int Stack::pop() {
  if (isEmpty()) throw std::out_of_range("Stack is empty, cannot pop.");
  int value = data.back();
  data.pop_back();
  return value;
}

int Stack::peek() const {
  if (isEmpty()) throw std::out_of_range("Stack is empty, cannot peek.");
  return data.back();
}
Key Takeaway

Edge-case tests make contracts explicit and prevent undefined behavior later in production.

screens.title: Common Testing Anti-Patterns
screens.subtitle: What to avoid and how to write maintainable tests

narration.text: As you write tests, be aware of anti-patterns that make suites brittle. First, testing implementation details ties tests to internal code paths; when you refactor internals the tests break even if behavior remains correct. Instead, assert on public behavior. Second, lack of isolation — when tests share mutable state — causes order-dependent failures. Use fixtures and per-test setup to avoid that. Third, over-mocking can make tests hard to understand; mock only when interactions with external dependencies cannot be tested reasonably, and prefer real objects for simple cases. Fourth, ignoring edge cases leads to untested failure modes; always add tests for boundaries, empty inputs, and exceptions. Finally, ignoring test failures reduces trust in the suite; a failing test is a signal that the code or test needs attention. Good tests are small, focused, readable, and fast. They make refactoring low-risk and keep the development loop fast. When in doubt, split a complex test into smaller parts and prefer clarity over clever shortcuts. Common Testing Anti-Patterns means focus on behavior, maintain isolation, mock judiciously, and cover edge cases to keep tests maintainable.. In practical terms, what to avoid and how to write maintainable tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid brittle tests
keyIdea.text: Focus on behavior, maintain isolation, mock judiciously, and cover edge cases to keep tests maintainable.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Common Testing Anti-Patterns
Anti-Patterns vs Safer Alternatives
Testing internals
Avoid asserting on private state or exact internal calls. Instead assert on public outcomes and observable behavior.
Shared mutable state
Avoid single global setup for many tests. Use fixtures so each test runs in a clean environment.
Over-mocking
Mock only when necessary. Prefer real objects for simple components to keep tests readable.
Skipping edge cases
Always include boundary and error-condition tests to document expected failures and prevent surprises.
Key Takeaway

Treat tests as code: keep them focused, independent, and clear so they remain a reliable safety net as your codebase evolves.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas to keep handy. Unit Testing is the practice of verifying small units—functions, methods, or classes—in isolation so behavior is specified and regressions are caught early. Google Test is a widely used framework for C++ that offers TEST and TEST_F, a rich assertion set, and fixture support to make tests expressive and maintainable. Assertions like EXPECT_EQ and ASSERT_THROW are the language tests use to declare expectations; choose ASSERT when a failure should stop further checks, EXPECT when you want to continue. These tools support Test Fixtures, which provide SetUp and TearDown to ensure test isolation and repeatability. Finally, Test-Driven Development follows Red-Green-Refactor to drive design: write a failing test, implement the minimal code to pass, then refactor. Keep cycles short, focus tests on behavior, and cover edge cases to produce a robust suite.

keyIdea.text: Tests are design tools: they document behavior, enable refactoring, and increase confidence.

screens.subtitle: Quick reference for practice and assessment

narration.text: A final compact reference: Test Fixture is the pattern to set up and clean resources before and after each test using SetUp and TearDown on a class derived from ::testing::Test. Test-Driven Development is the disciplined Red-Green-Refactor loop that drives design from failing tests. Red: add a failing test, Green: implement the simplest code to pass, Refactor: improve design while keeping tests green. Treat failing tests as signals to investigate; they point to either code regressions or test expectations that need updating. In practical assessments, use fixtures to initialize a UserManager or database mock for each test and prefer EXPECT when you can continue asserting multiple properties. Keep tests readable, focused, and fast so they remain a productive part of your development workflow. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation.
